They begin forming when a magma, which is cooling at depth, approaches the crystallization temperature of some of its minerals. These high-crystallization-temperature minerals begin forming below the surface and grow to visible sizes before the magma erupts. When the magma erupts onto the Earth's surface, the rest of the melt crystallizes quickly. Scoria forms from basaltic magmas, while pumice forms from rhyolitic magmas - which usually contain more gas. criteria.answer: kappa-mechanism: Explain that "kappa" refers to opacity. In the pulsation zone, Helium (He^+) is ionized to He^++ as the star contracts. Energy Trap: Ionized Helium is more opaque, trapping radiation and increasing internal pressure, which pushes the outer layers outward.Expansion & Cooling: As the star expands, it cools, and the Helium recombines (He^++ back to He^+), becoming transparent and allowing radiation to escape. Narrow Range: This only works in a speciﬁc temperature range where the Helium ionization zone is at the correct depth to drive the entire atmosphere.

O-type Stars: High surface temperatures (>30,000 K) cause atoms to be highly ionized. Features include He II (ionized helium) lines. M-type Stars: Cooler temperatures (<3,700 K) allow molecules to remain intact. Features include prominent Titanium Oxide (TiO) absorption bands. Molecular Dissociation: Explain that O-type stars have the same elements, but the intense heat provides enough energy to break molecular bonds (dissociation), meaning molecules like TiO cannot exist.

Core State: Core Hydrogen is exhausted, leaving an inert Helium core that begins to contract under gravity. Shell Burning: Hydrogen fusion moves to a shell surrounding the core, which provides the high luminosity and pressure that expands the envelope. Red Giant Growth: The envelope expands and cools (moving the star to the right), while the core becomes "electron degenerate." Degeneracy: In the core, electrons are packed so tightly that the Pauli Exclusion Principle provides pressure independent of temperature, preventing further collapse until the Helium Flash.

X-Ray (High Energy): Shows the "inner" nebula and the torus/jets. This emission is from the most energetic electrons recently accelerated by the pulsar. Radio (Low Energy): Shows the "outer" and more diffuse nebula. These are older electrons that have migrated further away and lost energy over time. Synchrotron Radiation: Both wavelengths are produced by electrons spiraling in magnetic ﬁelds; the difference in appearance is due to the electron's energy decay (synchrotron cooling).

Mie Scattering/Extinction: Dust grains are roughly the size of blue light wavelengths, so they scatter/absorb blue light more effectively than red (reddening). Optical Void: In the visible spectrum, the density of the dust is high enough to create inﬁnite optical depth (total obscuration). Infrared Advantage: IR wavelengths are much longer than the dust grain size, allowing them to pass through the cloud without being scattered. Protostar Identiﬁcation: IR allows us to see the thermal heat signature of the collapsing core (protostar) which is otherwise hidden.

Type II (Hydrogen Lines): Progenitor is a massive star (>8 M.) that retained its Hydrogen envelope before core collapse. Type Ia (Silicon, No Hydrogen): Progenitor is a White Dwarf in a binary system that reached the Chandrasekhar limit. It has no Hydrogen because White Dwarfs are the exposed cores of former stars. Evolutionary Path: Type II involves iron core collapse; Type Ia involves a thermonuclear runaway of Carbon/Oxygen.

Physical Structure: The "infrared excess" is caused by a circumstellar/protoplanetary disk of gas and dust that absorbs starlight and re-emits it as heat (IR). Evolutionary Stage: Unlike a protostar, a T Tauri star is visible in the optical, has cleared much of its "envelope," but is still contracting toward the Main Sequence. Hydrostatic Equilibrium: T Tauri stars have achieved a degree of hydrostatic balance but are powered by gravitational contraction rather than Hydrogen fusion.

Gravitational Settling: Because gravity is so intense, heavy elements (metals) sink to the center, leaving the lightest elements (H or He) at the surface. Spectral Types: DA white dwarfs have Hydrogen-rich atmospheres; DB have Helium-rich atmospheres. Janus Transition: Janus challenges this by showing "patches" or transitions, suggesting that as a star cools, convective zones can reach deep enough to "dredge up" buried Helium and mix the atmosphere.

Interacting Winds: A fast, thin wind from the hot white dwarf core catches up to the slow, dense wind ejected earlier during the AGB phase (the "snowplow" effect). Cometary Knots: These are dense clumps of molecular gas protected from the central star’s ionizing radiation by their own shadows, creating "tails" pointing away from the star. Ionization Fronts: The distinct "ring" shape is often an illusion of a 3D shell where the edges appear thicker from our line of sight.

Potential Energy Conversion: As matter falls from the donor star toward the compact object, it loses gravitational potential energy, which is converted into heat (kinetic energy). Accretion Disk Friction: Friction between different layers of the disk (differential rotation) generates temperatures in the millions of Kelvin.
